lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  SAUDI ARABIA AND YEMEN
lead.headline: Yemen's War Reaches Riyadh, and Washington Weighs Joining In
lead.deck: An attack on the Saudi capital's main airport killed at least 12 people. The fighting threatens the sea route Saudi oil now depends on.
body: Yemen's war reached the heart of Saudi Arabia on Saturday. An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and injured 309, the Saudi aviation authority said, among them travellers from Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan and the United States. Two days earlier a missile strike on the same airport killed three Saudis, one of them a pilot.

The likely attackers are the Houthis, the Iran-backed movement that has ruled northern Yemen since 2014. They claimed Thursday's strike and warned airlines to stay out of Saudi skies. Their missiles answer an offensive that Yemen's Saudi-backed government launched on October 4 to retake Houthi territory, backed by Saudi-led air strikes on Sanaa.

The fighting is now tangled up with the wider US-Iran war, in which no ceasefire is in force. Tehran says it expects a US reply to its latest proposal for a ceasefire and a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz; at a rally in Syracuse on Friday, Trump said he was "about to settle, or win" the war. At sea, 11 ships have been struck in or near the Strait of Hormuz so far this month, Fox News reported.
Asked whether the US would join, President Trump said: "We may. We're going to look at it." The UN's envoy for Yemen warned that the country has slid back into full-scale war.

map.title: BAB EL-MANDEB, THE GATE OF TEARS
map.footnote: About 30 km of water at its narrowest point
map.caption: With Hormuz disrupted, Saudi oil now leaves through this strait.

lead.why: For both India and the US the issue is energy. The Iran war has cut crude flowing through the Strait of Hormuz to about 40% below pre-war levels, and Brent crude closed near $104.50 on Friday, about two-thirds higher than a year ago. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its exports to the Red Sea, past the Bab el-Mandeb and the Yemeni coast the Houthis seized in September. India, which imports most of its oil, and an America three weeks from midterm elections both pay if that route closes too.

world.headline: A Daughter of Indian South Africa Wins the Peace Prize
world.deck: Navi Pillay helped build international criminal law. The US sanctioned the court she once served on the same day.
body: Navi Pillay was born in Durban in 1941, the daughter of a bus driver, in a country whose laws ranked people by race. As a lawyer she fought apartheid; as a judge she helped convict perpetrators of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, sat on the International Criminal Court (ICC) from 2003 to 2008, and served as UN human rights chief. On Friday, at 85, she won the Nobel Peace Prize. She will receive the prize, worth about one million euros, in Oslo on December 10.

The prize is contested. A UN panel she led concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies; Pillay has challenged her critics to say which of its facts are wrong. Prime Minister Netanyahu said the Nobel committee had "lost its moral compass". President Trump said the US "should have received" the prize and called Pillay someone "nobody has ever heard of". Pillay, who said she first thought the news "must be a joke", dedicated it to all the survivors of international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the US sanctioned the ICC itself, not just its officials, banning transactions with the court and potentially penalising companies that serve it. Washington objects to the court's investigation in Afghanistan, which could reach US personnel, and its arrest warrants for Israel's prime minister and former defence minister. The court called the move an assault on the rule of law; Japan, a close US ally, said it was deeply concerned.
Neither the United States nor India has joined the court, so the clash puts the two democracies on the same side of the membership line, if not the same side of the argument.

illustration.title: THE PEACE PRIZE
illustration.subtitle: Oslo, Norway
illustration.caption: Pillay dedicated the prize to the survivors of international crimes.

world.connect: Pillay's story begins with a voyage from India. From 1860, British colonial rulers shipped Indian labourers to Natal, the province around Durban, to cut sugar cane, and a large community of Indian descent grew there; Pillay, of Tamil heritage, is part of it. In 1893 a young lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi arrived in the same province, was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave a whites-only carriage, and spent two decades there learning to resist unjust laws without violence. A century apart, both concluded that the answer to injustice is law, not revenge.

india.headline: Delhi Seals Itself Off Against a Youth Protest Over Voter Lists
india.deck: More than 130 million names have been cut from India's electoral rolls. The opposition says real voters were purged; the Election Commission denies it.
body: India, with about a billion voters, has spent over a year re-checking its electoral rolls and struck off more than 130 million names. The opposition says genuine voters were removed to help Prime Minister Modi's BJP; the Election Commission and the BJP deny it.
Pressure on the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, grew after a newspaper reported that his own deputies had disagreed with him.
On Saturday a youth group that began as online satire, the Cockroach Janta Party, called a rally in New Delhi. Police refused permission, shut 57 metro stations and detained thousands.

illustration.title: DELHI'S PROTEST
illustration.subtitle: New Delhi, India
illustration.caption: 57 metro stations were shut to keep protesters away.

india.why: An election is only as fair as its voter list. Removing the dead is necessary; purging real voters wins without persuading anyone. The two can look alike, so trust in the referee matters.
also: The Reserve Bank of India raised its main interest rate to 5.50%, its first increase since February 2023.
India made 249 against the West Indies in Ranchi and still lost; the T20 series is level at 1-1.

us.headline: US Freezes Green-Card Filings at Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Five Others
us.deck: The Labor Department will not accept or process employer green-card applications from eight firms while it investigates alleged misuse.
body: For a foreign worker in America, an employer-sponsored green card usually starts with PERM, a Labor Department certification that no qualified American was available for the job. On Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling suspended eight companies from that programme: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe.

The department said it will neither accept new nor process pending applications from them, citing federal investigations into alleged misuse of immigration programmes and practices that could disadvantage American workers. The allegations are unproven. The suspension does not cancel existing H-1B visas or approved green cards.
Sonderling said the eight had received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications. Infosys said it expects no material impact.

chart.title: THE EIGHT FIRMS' TRACK RECORD
chart.subtitle: Approvals received, thousands (more than)
chart.caption: Figures cited by Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling.

us.why: Indian professionals are among the biggest users of these programmes, and many already wait years for a green card. A freeze at the largest Indian IT employers stalls pending cases, even for workers accused of nothing.
us.analyst: The department targeted employers, not visas. Ask what that changes: a worker's H-1B remains valid, but the path to permanent residence pauses. How might that affect who these firms can recruit, and whether workers stay?

items: Russia: President Trump said Russia will sell diesel to the US and waived sanctions on it until April 2027; Ukraine's president condemned the deal.
Florida: Hurricane Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 storm, killing at least four people and cutting power to more than 858,000 homes and businesses.

did_you_know.text: The US 'green card' is named after the pale green cards issued to permanent residents after 1946. Its colour changed several times over the decades before it turned green again in 2010.

sports.title: West Indies chase down 250 in Ranchi
sports.body: India made 249 for 5 in the second T20 international on Friday, with Sanju Samson hitting 82 off 41 balls. Shai Hope replied with an unbeaten 102 and Sherfane Rutherford made 84 as the West Indies reached 252 for 4 with nine balls left, their highest successful T20 chase. The five-match series is level at 1-1.
